question: Wait, why do we even have leap years? Is it just every four years, always?
speaker: other
expected_answer_type: accurate short spoken factual explanation
first_chunk: Because a year isn't a whole number of days
raw_answer:
Because a year isn't a whole number of days. Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to orbit the Sun, so we save up that extra quarter and add a day every four years to keep the calendar lined up with the seasons.

It's not quite that simple though. The quarter is a little short, so century years skip the leap day unless they're divisible by 400. That's why 2000 was a leap year but 1900 wasn't.

A credit report is the detailed record: your accounts, balances, payment history, and any collections or bankruptcies. A credit score is a number calculated from that report, so the report is the source and the score is the summary.

You can see both. Lenders, landlords, and insurers can see your report when you apply, and they see the score with it. Employers generally need your permission and see a version without your score.

A late payment typically stays about seven years from when it happened, though its impact fades as it ages.

question: I'm trying to decide between leasing a new car and buying a used one. I drive about 8,000 miles a year, I have about 6,000 saved, and I really hate dealing with repairs. Walk me through the trade-offs and tell me which way you'd lean.
speaker: user
expected_answer_type: trade-off comparison ending in a recommendation
first_chunk: At
raw_answer:
At 8,000 miles a year, you're a low-mileage driver, which is the key fact here. Leasing is usually priced around 10,000 to 12,000 miles a year, so you'd be paying for miles you won't use, and you'd still have a monthly payment forever with nothing to show at the end. Buying used means the car is yours once it's paid off, and at your mileage a well-chosen used car can last many years. The catch is repairs, which you hate. That's the real trade-off: a lease keeps you under warranty the whole time, while a used car eventually falls out of warranty and you're the one handling it.

With about 6,000 saved, I'd lean toward buying used, but a specific kind of used car: something a few years old, low miles, and with a reputation for reliability, ideally still under some factory warranty. Put your savings toward the down payment and keep a few thousand aside as a repair fund, so a surprise doesn't wreck you. If the idea of any repair at all is genuinely unbearable, a lease on a low-mileage plan can make sense, but you're paying a premium for that peace of mind and you'll never own anything.

[[GIST]] low miles favor buying used

Leasing is usually priced around 10,000 to 12,000 miles a year, so you'd be paying for miles you won't use, and you'd still have a monthly payment forever with nothing to show at the end. Buying used means the car is yours once it's paid off, and at your mileage a well-chosen used car can last many years. The catch is repairs, which you hate. That's the real trade-off: a lease keeps you under warranty the whole time, while a used car eventually falls out of warranty and you're the one handling it.

With about 6,000 saved, I'd lean toward buying used, but a specific kind of used car: something a few years old, low miles, and with a reputation for reliability, ideally still under some factory warranty. Put your savings toward the down payment and keep a few thousand aside as a repair fund, so a surprise doesn't wreck you. If the idea of any repair at all is genuinely unbearable, a lease on a low-mileage plan can make sense, but you're paying a premium for that peace of mind and you'll never own anything.

reference_file.title: Sourdough starter feeding schedule

expected_answer_type: simple fair splitting method
first_chunk: The
raw_answer:
The fairest quick way is to split it into three parts: what the two non-drinkers owe, what the big eater owes, and what everyone shares.

Practically: take the shared items (apps, bread, anything the table split) and divide those evenly by headcount. Then put the drinks on the drinkers' tab only, and the extra food the big eater ordered on theirs. Everyone pays their share of the shared stuff plus their own extras.

If that feels like too much math at the table, the easy version is to have the two non-drinkers pay just their share of the food, and the drinkers cover the alcohol and the oversized order between them.

"Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm [name], [brother's name]'s brother. speaker: user

expected_answer_type: two-sentence plain explanation
first_chunk: A
raw_answer:
A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and a server, so your traffic can't be read by anyone in between, like someone on the same Wi-Fi. It also makes your traffic appear to come from that server's location instead of your own, which hides your IP address from the sites you visit.

raw_answer:
Every record is split into fields, and each field carries its own version stamp, a hybrid logical clock value plus the device ID. So when two inspectors edit the same inspection offline, the server merges field by field. If they changed different fields, both edits survive. If they changed the same field, the higher clock wins, and the losing value goes to a conflict shelf the supervisor sees on the dashboard. Photos never conflict, they're append-only and keyed by a content hash, so a re-upload after a dropped connection is a no-op. In the first six months, 214 field-level conflicts hit the shelf, and supervisors overrode the automatic winner 9 times.

first_chunk: The ergodic hypothesis says that over long
raw_answer:
The ergodic hypothesis says that over long times, a single system's time average equals the average over all possible states at one instant. So instead of tracking one trajectory forever, you can average over an ensemble of copies at a fixed moment, which is usually far easier to compute. It's what lets statistical mechanics replace a hopeless many-body trajectory with a probability distribution. The catch is that it isn't true in general, systems with broken ergodicity, like glasses, can sit in one region of phase space for effectively forever.

question: A hash table gives you constant time lookup on average, but I want you to be suspicious of those two words, on average.
speaker: other
expected_answer_type: Explain what the caveat means and when it bites
first_chunk: The "on average" is doing real wo
raw_answer:
The "on average" is doing real work, and it's worth being precise about what it hides. Average-case O(1) assumes a good hash function and a load factor that stays bounded, so keys spread evenly across buckets. The moment either assumption breaks, you fall off a cliff: adversarial or poorly distributed keys collide into one bucket and lookup degrades to O(n), which is exactly the worst case an attacker can engineer. That's why real implementations don't trust the average. They resize and rehash as the load factor climbs, they use randomized or keyed hash functions so an attacker can't predict collisions, and some switch to a balanced tree per bucket to cap the worst case at O(log n). question: Walk me through deriving the quadratic formula by completing the square.
speaker: user
expected_answer_type: Step-by-step derivation with brief reasoning per step
first_chunk: Start
raw_answer:
Start from ax² + bx + c = 0 and divide everything by a, so x² + (b/a)x + c/a = 0. Move the constant over: x² + (b/a)x = -c/a. Half of b/a is b/2a, and squaring that gives b²/4a², so add it to both sides: x² + (b/a)x + b²/4a² = b²/4a² - c/a. The left side is now a perfect square, (x + b/2a)², and the right side combines to (b² - 4ac)/4a². Take the square root of both sides, x + b/2a = ±√(b² - 4ac)/2a, then subtract b/2a to get x = (-b ± √(b² - 4ac))/2a.

The intuition: completing the square turns the equation into "something squared equals a number," which you can just undo with a square root. The ± appears because both a positive and negative number square to the same value.

[[GIST]] complete the square, then take the root

question: What is entropy?
speaker: user
expected_answer_type: Short definition of the term
first_chunk: Ent
raw_answer:
Entropy is a measure of how many ways a system's microscopic parts can be arranged to produce the same overall state. The more arrangements that look the same from the outside, the higher the entropy.

In thermodynamics it's often described as disorder, but the cleaner idea is missing information: entropy counts the configurations you can't distinguish. The formula is **S = k log W**, where S is entropy, k is Boltzmann's constant, and W is the number of microstates matching the observed macrostate.

A simple example: a shuffled deck of cards has high entropy because almost every arrangement looks equally random, while a sorted deck has low entropy because only a few arrangements count as "sorted."

[[GIST]] entropy counts indistinguishable arrangements

prior_turns.text: Why does inflation hurt people who keep their money in savings?

Inflation means prices rise over time, so the same amount of cash buys less later than it does now. If your savings sit in an account earning less than the inflation rate, your money loses purchasing power even though the balance looks the same. Say inflation runs at 5% and your account pays 1%, you're effectively going backwards by about 4% a year in real terms. That's why people try to move savings into assets that grow faster than inflation.

expected_answer_type: Explain how expectations change the effect
first_chunk: If
raw_answer: If it's expected, people can plan around it. The damage is smaller because wages, contracts, and interest rates tend to adjust to anticipated inflation, so the real value of your savings erodes more slowly and predictably. The real harm comes from **unexpected inflation**, which catches everyone off guard and redistributes wealth from savers to borrowers.

question: What's the difference between mitosis and meiosis?
speaker: user
expected_answer_type: Side-by-side contrast of two processes
first_chunk: Mit
raw_answer:
Mitosis makes two cells that are **genetically identical** to the parent, and it's how the body grows and replaces worn-out cells. Meiosis makes four cells with **half the chromosomes**, and it's only for producing sperm and eggs. The key difference is that meiosis has two rounds of division after one round of DNA copying, and it shuffles the genes through crossing over, so every gamete ends up genetically unique.

[[GIST]] mitosis clones, meiosis halves and shuffles

question: Consider the prisoner's dilemma.
speaker: other
expected_answer_type: Brief primer on the named concept
first_chunk: The prisoner's dilemma is a setup where two
raw_answer:
The prisoner's dilemma is a setup where two people each choose to cooperate or defect, and the payoffs are arranged so that defecting is always better for you no matter what the other person does, yet if you both defect you both end up worse off than if you'd both cooperated. The classic story is two suspects interrogated separately: each is tempted to confess for a lighter sentence, but if both confess they both get a longer sentence than if both stayed quiet. The tension is that the individually rational choice leads to a collectively worse outcome, which is why it's the standard model for why cooperation is hard without trust or repeated interaction.

[[GIST]] individual rationality, collectively worse outcome

Mutual defection is a Nash equilibrium because neither player can improve by unilaterally switching: if the other is defecting, defecting is your best response, so neither has an incentive to move. question: Derive the kinetic energy formula from the definition of work.
speaker: user
expected_answer_type: Step-by-step derivation from first principles
first_chunk: Work
raw_answer:
Work is force times displacement, so for a constant force along the direction of motion, \(W = F\,d\). Using Newton's second law, \(F = ma\), and the kinematic relation \(v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ad\), we get \(d = \frac{v^2 - v_0^2}{2a}\). Substituting both into the work expression gives \(W = ma \cdot \frac{v^2 - v_0^2}{2a} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_0^2\). That difference is the change in kinetic energy, so \(KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\), where \(m\) is mass and \(v\) is speed. The intuition is that the work you do on an object shows up as a change in this quantity.

[[GIST]] work equals change in half mv squared

expected_answer_type: Extend the derivation to a non-constant force
first_chunk: If
raw_answer:
If the force isn't constant, you can't just multiply \(F\) by \(d\). You split the path into tiny pieces where the force is roughly constant, so each piece contributes \(F\,dx\), and the total work is the integral \(W = \int F\,dx\). So the same result holds, the half survives, and the work-energy theorem still says work equals the change in kinetic energy.

A multiplier is just a number you multiply by to scale something up or down. If a base value is 200 and the multiplier is 1.5, the result is 300. If it's 0.5, the result is 100.

In most lectures it shows up in one of two ways: as a scaling factor in a formula, like output equals input times the multiplier, or as a feedback effect, where a small change gets amplified because it feeds back into itself. The key intuition is that a multiplier above 1 grows the thing, below 1 shrinks it, and exactly 1 leaves it unchanged.

[[GIST]] multiplier scales a value up or down

Glycolysis happens in the cytosol: one glucose goes in, two pyruvate, 2 ATP and 2 NADH come out. question: And the reason you can't skip breathing is that oxygen is the final electron acceptor, that's its whole job.
speaker: other

expected_answer_type: Explain the term and why oxygen matters, per the notes
first_chunk: Right, oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor
raw_answer:
Right, oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain. Electrons passed down the chain from NADH and FADH2 get handed off to oxygen, which combines with protons to form water. Without that final step, the chain backs up, NADH can't be reoxidized back to NAD+, and the whole process stalls. So no oxygen means no electron flow, which means no proton gradient, and without the gradient ATP synthase has nothing to drive it. That's why breathing isn't optional for aerobic respiration.

[[GIST]] oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor
rendered_answer:
That's right, and the notes back it up: oxygen is the final electron acceptor and ends up as water. Without it the chain backs up and the earlier stages stall. The reason you can't just skip it is that nothing else can take those electrons at the end, so NADH and FADH2 have nowhere to drop them and the whole process jams. The payoff is roughly 2.5 ATP per NADH and about 1.5 ATP per FADH2, so around 30 to 32 ATP per glucose.

[[GIST]] oxygen accepts electrons, becomes water

raw_answer:
The spinning jenny and the water frame solved different problems, which is why you need both to get to the factory. The jenny, from Hargreaves, multiplied the number of threads a single spinner could draw, so it sped up spinning but still ran on human power and stayed in the home or small workshop. The water frame, from Arkwright, used rollers to spin stronger thread and was driven by water power, so it forced production out of the cottage and into a building next to a river. Put them together and you get the two ingredients the factory system needs: a machine that outproduces hand spinning, and a power source that can't fit in a cottage. question: What is a limiting reagent, how do I spot one in a problem, and can you walk me through a quick example?
speaker: user

reference_file.title: Campus parking closure notice

expected_answer_type: Definition, identification method and a short worked example
first_chunk: A
raw_answer:
A limiting reagent is the reactant that runs out first and so caps how much product you can make. To spot it, convert every reactant's amount to moles, divide each by its coefficient in the balanced equation, and the smallest result is your limiting reagent. For example, in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, if you have 3 mol H₂ and 2 mol O₂, then H₂ gives 3/2 = 1.5 and O₂ gives 2/1 = 2, so H₂ limits and you get 3 mol H₂O.

[[GIST]] smallest mole-to-coefficient ratio limits

question: So the workhorse here is stochastic gradient descent, and I'm not going to derive it today, just take it on faith.
speaker: other

reference_file.title: Campus parking closure notice

expected_answer_type: Explain the concept the lecturer skipped over
first_chunk: Stochastic gradient descent is the update
raw_answer: Stochastic gradient descent is the update rule that trains most of these models: instead of computing the gradient over the whole dataset, you estimate it from one example, or a small batch, and take a step. So the update is **θ ← θ − η ∇L(θ; xᵢ, yᵢ)**, where θ is the parameters, η is the learning rate, and ∇L is the gradient of the loss on that single example. The intuition is that each noisy step is cheap and roughly points downhill, so you make many quick steps instead of a few expensive exact ones, and the noise itself helps you move around.

question: How is a virus different from a bacterium?
speaker: user

reference_file.title: Campus parking closure notice

expected_answer_type: Concise contrast of two biological entities
first_chunk: A
raw_answer:
A virus isn't a cell at all. It's just genetic material, either DNA or RNA, wrapped in a protein coat, and it has no ribosomes or metabolism of its own, so it can't reproduce or make proteins by itself. It has to hijack a host cell's machinery to copy itself.

A bacterium is a living single-celled organism. It has its own ribosomes, a cell membrane, and can carry out metabolism and reproduce on its own, usually by dividing. That's also why antibiotics work on bacteria but not on viruses: antibiotics target bacterial structures like the cell wall or ribosomes, which viruses simply don't have.

[[GIST]] virus not a cell, bacterium is

speaker: other

reference_file.title: Campus parking closure notice

expected_answer_type: Explain the deadweight loss idea in plain language
first_chunk: That's the right intuition, with one refinement
raw_answer:
That's the right intuition, with one refinement worth making. The monopolist restricts output to where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and charges the price the demand curve supports at that quantity. The deadweight loss isn't the gap in quantity itself, it's the lost surplus on the units that would have been produced and consumed between the monopoly quantity and the competitive quantity, where willingness to pay still exceeds marginal cost. So it's the area of the triangle between the demand curve and the marginal cost curve over that range, not a count of missing units.

[[GIST]] deadweight loss is lost surplus, not missing units

question: array vs linked list, when would I actually pick the linked list?
speaker: user
expected_answer_type: Honest comparison with realistic cases for each
first_chunk: A
raw_answer:
A linked list wins when you need **O(1) insertions and deletions** at a position you already hold a reference to, and you don't need random access. Arrays give you O(1) indexing but shifting elements on insert or delete is O(n), so if you're doing a lot of splicing in the middle of a structure, a linked list avoids that cost.

The tradeoff is cache behavior and memory overhead. Arrays are contiguous, so iteration is fast and cache-friendly. Linked lists scatter nodes across the heap, each with a pointer, so traversal is slower in practice and you pay extra memory per node. In most real workloads the array still wins because of that locality.

So I'd reach for a linked list when the access pattern is genuinely insert-heavy or delete-heavy at known positions, like an LRU cache with a doubly linked list, or a queue where you're only touching the ends. Otherwise the array or a dynamic array is the safer default.

raw_answer:
A binary search tree is a binary tree where every node's left subtree holds smaller keys and its right subtree holds larger ones, so search, insert, and delete run in time proportional to the tree's height. Inserting one through a thousand in sorted order is the worst case: each new value is larger than everything before it, so it always goes to the rightmost position and the tree degenerates into a linked list of a thousand nodes. That makes height n instead of log n, so lookups and inserts drop from about ten comparisons to a thousand. A self-balancing tree like a red-black or AVL tree avoids this by rotating to keep height logarithmic.

first_chunk: Coll
raw_answer:
Collisions happen when two keys hash to the same bucket, and there are two main ways to handle them.

**Chaining** keeps a list at each bucket. Every key that lands there gets appended, so lookups scan that short list. It's simple, handles high load factors gracefully, and deletion is easy.

**Open addressing** stores everything in the table itself. On a collision you probe for the next free slot, either linearly, quadratically, or with double hashing. It's more cache-friendly and uses less memory, but deletions need tombstones and performance degrades fast as the table fills.

[[GIST]] chaining uses lists, open addressing probes

question: So building a heap from an array is n log n, right? Walk me through why.
speaker: other
expected_answer_type: Address the premise then walk through the reasoning
first_chunk: Not quite. Building a heap from an
raw_answer:
Not quite. Building a heap from an array is actually **O(n)**, not O(n log n). The n log n figure comes from doing n separate insertions, but heapify works differently.

The key is that heapify sifts down from the last internal node up to the root. The cost of sifting down depends on the height of the node, and most nodes are near the bottom where the height is small. Only a few nodes near the root have large heights.

If you sum the work across all levels, you get n/2 nodes doing 1 swap, n/4 doing 2, n/8 doing 3, and so on. That series converges to a constant times n, so the total is **O(n)**.

The n log n bound is a loose upper bound, but the tight bound is linear.

speaker: user
expected_answer_type: Numbered spoken steps for the approach, no code
first_chunk: For
raw_answer:
For permutations, I'd use backtracking. The idea is to build the result one position at a time, and at each position try every remaining element.

1. Keep a current partial permutation and a set of which elements are already used.
2. At each step, loop over the elements not yet used, add one, and recurse.
3. When the partial permutation is the same length as the input, record a copy of it as a complete result.
4. After each recursive call, remove the element you just added so the next choice starts clean.

That's the core. If the list has duplicates and you want unique permutations, sort first and skip an element when it equals the previous one and that previous one wasn't used at this level. The cost is factorial in the length, since there are n! results.

[[GIST]] backtrack, try unused, recurse, undo

first_chunk: The
raw_answer:
The bug is a data race: all 100 goroutines read and write `total` with no synchronization, so increments get lost. There's also a closure bug, since `i` is captured by reference and may be read after the loop advances.

```go
func main() {
	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	var mu sync.Mutex
	total := 0
	for i := 1; i <= 100; i++ {
		wg.Add(1)
		go func(i int) {
			defer wg.Done()
			mu.Lock()
			total += i
			mu.Unlock()
		}(i)
	}
	wg.Wait()
	fmt.Println(total)
}
```

Passing `i` as a parameter fixes the capture, and the mutex serializes the writes. For a single counter, an atomic is the better fix: `atomic.AddInt64(&total, int64(i))` is lock-free and cheaper than a mutex, which only pays off when you're protecting a larger critical section.

question: Let's design a chat application like WhatsApp. It needs one to one and group messages, delivery and read receipts, and online presence, and it has to work for a few hundred million users. Where do you start, and what are the main components?
speaker: other
expected_answer_type: Structured design opening with requirements, components and key trade-offs
first_chunk: I'd start by separating the two planes: the
raw_answer:
I'd start by separating the two planes: the message plane and the presence plane, because they have very different consistency needs. For messages, each user gets a durable per-device inbox, and a message is written once with a server-assigned ID and monotonic sequence, then fanned out to recipients. For a few hundred million users, that fan-out is the hard part, so I'd shard by user ID and keep a routing layer that maps a user to the gateway holding their live connection.

The main components: a connection gateway layer holding persistent sockets, a session or presence service tracking who's online, a message service that persists and orders messages, a fan-out or delivery service, a group service that expands a group send into per-member deliveries, and a receipt service for delivered and read states. Storage splits into a hot store for recent messages and a cold store for history, with per-conversation ordering.

For receipts and presence, I'd treat them as best-effort signals rather than durable facts. Delivery and read receipts are just small state updates keyed by message and user, and presence is a heartbeat with a TTL, so a dropped connection expires on its own instead of needing an explicit offline event. Group fan-out is the scaling risk, so I'd cap group size or fan out lazily for very large groups, and I'd make the whole path idempotent with client-generated IDs so retries don't duplicate messages.

[[GIST]] split message and presence planes, shard by user

question: walk me through designing dropbox at a high level, focus on syncing big files
speaker: user
expected_answer_type: High-level design centred on chunked file sync
first_chunk: Here
raw_answer:
Here's how I'd approach it. The core is a **chunked, content-addressed store**: split each file into fixed or content-defined chunks, hash each one, and store chunks by hash so identical data is deduplicated and only changed chunks move. A metadata service tracks the file tree, chunk lists, and versions, while the actual bytes live in blob storage.

For syncing big files, the key is **delta sync**: when a file changes, the client re-chunks it, compares hashes against what the server already has, and uploads only the new chunks. That way editing one region of a multi-gigabyte file doesn't re-upload the whole thing. Content-defined chunking helps here because it keeps chunk boundaries stable when bytes are inserted or removed, so fewer chunks shift.

On the client side I'd run a watcher that detects changes and a sync engine that queues uploads, with resumable transfers so a dropped connection picks up mid-file rather than restarting. The server needs to handle concurrent edits, so I'd version files and detect conflicts, keeping both copies when two clients diverge. For scale, chunks go to a distributed blob store, metadata to a replicated database, and clients get notified of changes via a long-poll or push channel so they pull only what changed.

first_chunk: Offset
raw_answer:
Offset pagination breaks down at that scale: the database still has to walk and discard every skipped row, so deep pages get slow, and rows shifting between requests cause duplicates or gaps. Cursor pagination fixes both. You encode the last row's sort key, usually an indexed column like id or created_at, and the next query becomes a simple "where key > last key" with a limit, so it's a constant-time index seek no matter how deep you are.

The tradeoff is you lose random access, so no jumping to page 500, and the cursor has to be opaque and stable. For a feed or infinite scroll, cursor wins. If the client genuinely needs page numbers, offset is fine for shallow pages only.

question: Minimum window substring. You get two strings, s and t. Find the smallest substring of s that contains every character of t, counting duplicates. How would you solve it?
speaker: other
expected_answer_type: Sliding window approach explained step by step, spoken
raw_answer:
## Approach
Sliding window with two pointers and a frequency count. Expand the right pointer until the window covers all of t, then shrink from the left while it still covers t, recording the smallest valid window. A `need` map tracks required counts and a `have`/`missing` counter tells you when the window is valid.

## Code
```python
from collections import Counter

def minWindow(s: str, t: str) -> str:
    if not t or not s:
        return ""
    need = Counter(t)
    required = len(need)
    formed = 0
    window = {}
    left = 0
    best = (float("inf"), 0, 0)

    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        window[ch] = window.get(ch, 0) + 1
        if ch in need and window[ch] == need[ch]:
            formed += 1

        while formed == required:
            if right - left + 1 < best[0]:
                best = (right - left + 1, left, right)
            lc = s[left]
            window[lc] -= 1
            if lc in need and window[lc] < need[lc]:
                formed -= 1
            left += 1

    return "" if best[0] == float("inf") else s[best[1]:best[2] + 1]
```

## Complexity
Time is O(n + m) where n is the length of s and m is the length of t, since each pointer moves at most n times. Space is O(k) for the frequency maps, where k is the number of distinct characters.

question: Explain how quicksort works and why the worst case is quadratic.
speaker: other

reference_file.title: Facilities notice: kitchen renovation

expected_answer_type: Spoken explanation of partitioning and the worst-case input
first_chunk: Quicksort picks a pivot elemen
raw_answer:
Quicksort picks a pivot element, then partitions the array so everything smaller than the pivot sits to its left and everything larger sits to its right. It then recurses on both sides. With a good pivot, each partition splits the array roughly in half, so you get about log n levels of recursion, and each level does O(n) work scanning and swapping, giving **O(n log n)** on average.

The worst case comes from unbalanced splits. If the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, like when you pick the first element of an already sorted array, each partition peels off just one element. That gives n levels of recursion instead of log n, and since each level still costs O(n), the total is **O(n²)**. Randomized or median-of-three pivot selection makes that case very unlikely.

[[GIST]] pivot, partition, unbalanced splits cause O(n²)

I'd go hybrid: fan-out on write for normal accounts, and pull at read time for the big ones. When someone posts, a fan-out service pushes the post id into the timeline caches of their followers, so opening the app is just a read of a precomputed list. That keeps reads fast and cheap.

So a read pulls the precomputed timeline plus a small query against those big accounts, then merges and ranks.

```python
def consolidate_region
raw_answer:
```python
def consolidate_region(windows):
    """Consolidate overlapping or touching windows for a single region.

    windows: iterable of (start, end) tuples, unsorted, may contain duplicates.
    Returns a new list of (start, end) tuples sorted by start, input untouched.
    """
    ordered = sorted(windows)
    merged = []
    for start, end in ordered:
        if merged and start <= merged[-1][1]:
            if end > merged[-1][1]:
                merged[-1] = (merged[-1][0], end)
        else:
            merged.append((start, end))
    return merged
```

Sorting first makes the merge a single linear pass, and `start <= merged[-1][1]` is what catches the touching case where one window ends exactly when the next begins. It builds a fresh list, so the input is never mutated.

Time O(n log n), space O(n).

question: in my session cache file, a session I update with put() disappears way earlier than the ttl. find the bug
speaker: user

reference_file.title: Candidate's own code file: session_cache.py

expected_answer_type: Locate the cause in the attached code and give a minimal fix
first_chunk: The
raw_answer:
The bug is in `put()` on the update path. When the key already exists, it overwrites the value and refreshes recency, but it never resets `self.expires[key]`. So the entry keeps the expiry from the original write, and it dies at the original ttl even though you just put it again. The fix is to set `self.expires[key] = time.time() + self.ttl` in that branch too, before returning.

```python
def put(self, key, value):
    if key in self.values:
        self.values[key] = value
        self.expires[key] = time.time() + self.ttl
        self.order.remove(key)
        self.order.append(key)
        return
```

That also explains why your tests missed it: none of them updates an existing key, so the stale-expiry path never runs.

[[GIST]] update path never refreshes expiry

question: Let's do the shortlink service in the brief you have. Cover the API, how you store the links, how you generate the codes, and how it scales.
speaker: other

reference_file.title: System design brief: Shortlinks service

expected_answer_type: Structured design using the brief's numbers and requirements
first_chunk: I'll start with the API, then storage, code
raw_answer:
I'll start with the API, then storage, code generation, and scaling.

**API.** Two main endpoints. `POST /links` takes the long URL, an optional custom alias up to 30 characters, and an optional expiry date, and returns the short code. `GET /{code}` does the redirect. I'd also add a `GET /links/{code}/stats` for the dashboard. On create, I check the alias isn't taken and that the target domain isn't on the abuse list before writing.

**Storage.** A key-value store keyed by short code, with the long URL, expiry, and owner. At 30 million new links a month and 500 bytes per record, that's roughly 15 GB a month, so about 900 GB over five years. Reads are 100 to 1 over writes, so this is read-heavy and I'd keep it in a store that can serve lookups from memory, with the code as the primary key.

**Code generation.** I'd generate a random base62 code, 7 characters, which gives about 3.5 trillion combinations, so collisions are rare. On insert I check for a collision and retry if needed. Custom aliases go through the same uniqueness check.

**Scaling.** Redirects are the hot path, so I'd put a cache in front of the store, since the same links get clicked repeatedly. For a link that suddenly goes viral, the cache absorbs the load and the store stays protected. Click events go to a queue and get aggregated into daily counts, which is fine since the brief says counts can be a little late. For the 100 to 1 read ratio and five times peak, I'd scale the redirect tier horizontally and keep the write path separate so link creation doesn't compete with redirects.

[[GIST]] API, KV storage, base62 codes, cache for scale

On insert I write with the code as the key and check for a collision, retrying with a fresh code if one comes back. At that space size collisions are rare, so it's usually one attempt. Custom aliases skip generation and go through the same uniqueness check.
What about duplicate URLs?

Two customers shortening the same long URL should get separate codes, since each one needs its own click counts and its own expiry. So I don't dedupe on the URL. If someone wants the same link back, I'd let them reuse their existing code rather than mint a new one, but that's a lookup by owner, not a global constraint.

expected_answer_type: Plain-language general explanation, easy to say aloud
first_chunk: A
raw_answer:
A confidence interval is a range of values that's likely to contain the true value we're estimating, along with a stated level of confidence. If I say a 95% confidence interval for a mean runs from 4.2 to 5.8, it means that if we repeated the same sampling procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals we built that way would capture the true mean. It's not a 95% chance that the true value sits in this particular interval, and it's not a range of the data itself. The width tells you how precise the estimate is: narrower means more precise, and it usually tightens as the sample grows or the data varies less.

question: Why defer compaction at all? Why not just compact as soon as the threshold is hit?
speaker: other

expected_answer_type: Explain rationale drawing on motivation and method sections
first_chunk: Because compacting the moment the threshold
raw_answer:
Because compacting the moment the threshold is hit means compaction competes with foreground writes for the same device bandwidth, which is exactly when write amplification and read tail latency get worse. TidalLog instead computes the tide as the recent foreground write rate over the smoothed sustainable rate, and when that's above 0.7 it defers level 2 and deeper for up to three windows, 15 seconds. Level 0 is exempt, so it still compacts at 8 files and stalls at 12.

question: Can you explain what a random effect is, for those of us outside statistics?
speaker: other

reference_file.title: Slide deck: tone sandhi in Ostrelle compound nouns (linguistics)

expected_answer_type: General plain explanation that ignores unrelated attached material
first_chunk: A random effect is a way of letting each
raw_answer: A random effect is a way of letting each group in your data have its own baseline, instead of forcing them all to share one. Say you're measuring students across many schools: a fixed effect would give you one average for everyone, while a random effect lets each school shift up or down around that average, and it treats those shifts as draws from a common distribution rather than as separate things you want to estimate. The practical payoff is that you're not burning a parameter on every group, and groups with little data get pulled toward the overall mean.
